props.title: Once Upon a Time in the West
props.initialSlug: Epic revenge tale reshapes the dying Old West

sections.content: Once Upon a Time in the West represents Sergio Leone's masterful culmination of the Spaghetti Western genre. Leone deliberately subverts expectations by casting Henry Fonda, Hollywood's quintessential good guy, as the cold-blooded killer Frank. The film's opening sequence at the train station - nearly 15 minutes with barely any dialogue - showcases Leone's genius for building tension through extreme close-ups, Ennio Morricone's haunting score, and the methodical pacing that would influence directors like Quentin Tarantino in Reservoir Dogs (1992) and The Hateful Eight (2015).

sections.content: The film's epic scope draws from classical Western mythology while simultaneously deconstructing it. Charles Bronson's mysterious Harmonica represents the genre's traditional revenge narrative, but Leone frames it within a broader story about the death of the Old West and the arrival of civilization. This theme would later influence modern Westerns like Unforgiven (1992) and The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (2007), which similarly examine the West's transition and mythmaking.

Claudia Cardinale's Jill McBain breaks from traditional Western female roles, emerging as a central figure in the modernization narrative rather than a simple love interest. This characterization influenced later revisionist Westerns like The Quick and the Dead (1995) and Meek's Cutoff (2010), which similarly challenged genre conventions about gender roles. sections.content: Leone and cinematographer Tonino Delli Colli's revolutionary use of extreme close-ups and wide shots created a visual language that transcended the Western genre. Their technique of cutting from vast landscapes to extreme facial close-ups influenced films like The Revenant (2015) and No Country for Old Men (2007). Morricone's score, giving each character their own musical theme, established a template for character-specific leitmotifs that would influence composers like John Williams and Hans Zimmer.
